intro: Three of these trees make a short walk in central Funchal: an araucaria in the grounds of Quinta Vigia, the president's official residence, free and open on weekdays, and an ombu and a camphor tree a few streets away in the Jardim Municipal. Five more are spread around the city, from the botanical garden to the dragon trees at Neves and the hillside estate at Palheiro. Only two are real drives, Queimadas above Santana and the til grove at Fanal, an hour or more in opposite directions. Eight of the ten carry no recorded age at all.
meta_description: Madeira's ten remarkable trees: three a short walk apart in central Funchal, a witch-shaped til in the Fanal laurel forest and a dragon tree grove.
question_meta: Madeira's oldest listed tree is the Witch Tree in the til grove at Fanal, several hundred years old. The Funchal giants carry no recorded age.
question_answer: The oldest tree on this list is the Witch Tree at Fanal, a til (Ocotea foetens) in the protected grove on the Paul da Serra plateau above Porto Moniz. Estimates for it run from several hundred years to 500 or 600, and Madeira's own register dates the grove around it only as centenas de anos, hundreds of years, describing a stand referenced as predating the Portuguese settlement of the island in 1419. That is the loosest kind of answer and it is the best one available, because the other eight trees on this list carry no recorded age at all.
question_context: Madeira barely records ages for its monumental trees. Eight of the ten here have none, from two different lists. The island's own inventory gives the ginkgo, the cypress at Quinta Magnolia, the copper beech at Monte and the Douglas fir at Queimadas a height, a trunk perimeter and a condition, then writes sem referencia, no reference, in the age column. Funchal's municipal list is thinner still: the araucaria at Quinta Vigia, the ombu and camphor tree in the Jardim Municipal and the pohutukawa at Palheiro appear as a code and a name, from a 2008 regional survey, with no measurement at all. That leaves the two native stands. The dragon trees at Neves are centenarios, over a century, and no more precisely. The til grove at Fanal is dated only as centenas de anos, hundreds of years, and referenced as predating the Portuguese arrival in 1419; tourism sources put the Witch Tree at 500 or 600 years with nothing published behind the number. So the honest ranking is Fanal first, Neves second, eight undated trees after them. The Douglas fir is the trap: tallest here at 39 metres, and Douglas firs grow fast.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Madeira?
faq.a: Of the trees on this list, the Witch Tree in the til grove at Fanal, on the Paul da Serra plateau above Porto Moniz. The register dates the grove only as hundreds of years and references it as predating the settlement of the island in 1419; tourism sources put the individual tree at 500 or 600 years without publishing any working.

faq.q: Why do so many of Madeira's monumental trees have no age?
faq.a: Because the lists they come from record size, or nothing at all. The island's inventory gives each entry a height, a trunk perimeter and a condition, and against the ginkgo, the cypress at Quinta Magnolia, the copper beech at Monte and the Douglas fir at Queimadas the age column reads sem referencia, no reference. Funchal's municipal list, which is where the araucaria, the ombu, the camphor tree and the pohutukawa come from, carries a code and a name and no measurements whatsoever. Nobody has cored any of them. If you have a planting record for one, we would like it.

faq.q: Do you need a car, and how far apart are these trees?
faq.a: Three of them are a walk. The araucaria at Quinta Vigia on Avenida do Infante and the ombu and camphor tree in the Jardim Municipal stand within about a kilometre of each other in central Funchal, all free, and you can see the three in a morning on foot; Quinta Vigia is government grounds and opens Monday to Friday only, so make it a weekday. Five more need a bus, the cable car or a short taxi ride: the botanical garden, Quinta Magnolia, the Emperor's Garden at Monte, the dragon trees at Neves, and Palheiro Gardens up in the hills to the east, which charges 11 euros. Only two need a car. Queimadas at Santana is about an hour's drive, and Fanal is an hour and a quarter of mountain road across the Paul da Serra plateau in the opposite direction.

faq.q: Is the Witch Tree at Fanal signposted?
faq.a: No. There is no sign, no arrow and no marked path to it, and visitors regularly report hunting around the grove before they find it. Our pin marks the part of the grove it stands in rather than the trunk itself. Morning fog is when Fanal looks the way it does in photographs.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Botanical Garden

location.address: Jardim Botânico da Madeira Eng.º Rui Vieira, Caminho do Meio, Funchal

trees.story:
Madeira's official register of monumental trees records this ginkgo for exactly one reason, size, and where the age should go it says sem referencia, no reference. Nobody has dated it. What the surveyors did measure is 18 metres of height and a trunk 1.62 metres round, which is a substantial specimen of a tree that has no obvious business thriving at this latitude and manages it anyway.

Ginkgo biloba is the last species left of an entire lineage, with no close living relative anywhere, and it reached European gardens only in the eighteenth century. This one grows in the Jardim Botanico da Madeira on the slope above Funchal, among roughly 3,000 species pulled in from every continent the garden could reach, ten minutes out of the city by bus or a cable car ride down from Monte.

The garden opened to the public in 1960, which dates the garden and not the tree. Nobody has recorded when this ginkgo went in. If you have a planting record, or a girth measured more recently than the survey, send it to us.

And then in November the crown turns butter gold and drops the lot inside a few days, which is the week to be standing under it.

best_time.label: November, when the crown turns gold and drops it in a few days

trees.access: Paid entry, EUR 7.50 adult, open daily 09:00-18:00 (last admission 30 min before close)
trees.transport: Bus 29, 30, 31 or 31A from central Funchal (about 10 minutes), or the Teleférico do Jardim Botânico cable car from Monte. No car needed for this one.
trees.notes: Register entry ASMAC n.87/90 (island code FSMMGB01), the IFCN/VALCONMAC official inventory of Madeira's singular and monumental trees (Duarte Olim survey, undated but citing the 2018/2021 regional legal framework for monumental trees). Height 18.0m, maximum perimeter 1.62m (162cm), notable reason 'Tamanho' (size). No age reference given in the register ('Sem referencia'); the garden itself opened to the public in 1960 but that is the garden's founding, not a documented planting date for this specific tree, so age stays undocumented per the bridge-claim rule and the story states the distinction explicitly. One large ginkgo is catalogued among the garden's collection of roughly 3000 species; second source is the garden's own official visitor-information page confirming continued public operation, hours and fee, not a tree-specific corroboration. Flagged because the second source verifies the site rather than the individual specimen; the register is otherwise a single official government source. Alive: garden actively operating in 2026 per its own site. best_time set from data/phenology/ginkgo.json, which rates the autumn colour 'worth the trip'.
trees.how_to_recognise: Eighteen metres on a trunk 1.62 metres round, the one tree in the garden with fan-shaped leaves in two lobes; in November it drops the whole gold crown within days.

trees.name: The Cypress of Quinta Magnolia

location.address: Quinta Magnólia, Rua Dr. Pita, Funchal

trees.story:
Madeirans call this species cedro-das-barracas, the shed cedar, because the young leading shoot was traditionally cut off so the crown would thicken outward into a roof of shade. Nobody did that to this one. It went up instead: 29.5 metres tall on a trunk 6.06 metres around, more than a metre of solid diameter, which the island's register singles out as exceptional for a Cupressus lusitanica and enough to make it one of the largest of its kind on Madeira.

The species is not Portuguese, whatever the name says. It comes from Mexico and Central America, and it took its Latin name from trees already growing in Portugal rather than from anywhere near its actual origin.

Its age is not recorded. The register gives its condition as bom, good, and notes that it is under permanent technical monitoring, which is what the island does with trees it has no intention of losing. Nobody has dated it, and if you know when it was planted, tell us.

It stands in Quinta Magnolia, a public park of some 40,000 square metres in the middle of Funchal, free and open from eight in the morning until eight at night, which makes this the easiest tree on the list to go and see.
trees.transport: Central Funchal park, walkable from the Lido seafront area or a short bus or taxi ride from the city centre. No car needed for this one.
trees.notes: Register entry ASMAC n.92 (island code FSMCL01). Height 29.5m, maximum perimeter 6.06m (606cm), notable reason 'Tamanho' (size), condition 'Bom' (good) with permanent technical monitoring. The register calls it one of the largest specimens of its species on the island, over 1m trunk diameter and 30m+ height being noted as exceptional for Cupressus lusitanica. No age reference in the register; locally known as 'cedro-das-barracas' because its young leader shoot was traditionally cut to thicken the crown into a shade bower. Second source (lifecooler.com, corroborated by visitmadeira.com and madeira-web.com) confirms Quinta Magnolia as a real, currently operating 40,000sqm public park with free entry 08:00-20:00, but does not name this specific tree, so flagged as site-level rather than tree-specific corroboration, same caveat as mdr_001. Alive: park in active public use in 2026. Species string trimmed at write time from 'Mexican Cypress (Cupressus lusitanica), locally cedro-das-barracas' to the canonical common+Latin form; the local name moved into the story.
trees.how_to_recognise: Twenty-nine metres up on a trunk six metres round, grown tall rather than spread wide, which is the opposite of what this species is usually cut to do here.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Emperor's Garden

location.address: Quinta Jardins do Imperador, Beco do Pico, Monte, Funchal

trees.story:
The last Emperor of Austria died in this garden. Karl I, deposed in 1918 and exiled to Madeira, spent his final months at what was then Quinta do Monte and died there in 1922, which is why the estate is now the Jardins do Imperador, the Emperor's Garden.

The tree that dominates it is a copper beech, 36 metres tall on a trunk 3.52 metres round. That is an odd thing to find here. Fagus sylvatica is a northern European forest tree and this is a subtropical island in the Atlantic; what makes it possible is Monte itself, high on the slope above Funchal in the belt of cloud that the trade winds push up against the mountain. The parish is permanently damp and several degrees cooler than the seafront, and the beech behaves accordingly.

Madeira's monumental tree register lists it for size, records its condition as good, and gives its age as sem referencia, no reference. Nobody has dated it, and the estate's own history does not settle it. If you know when this beech was planted, tell us.

Entry costs around a euro, often nothing on Sundays, and the Monte cable car from Funchal stops a short walk away.
trees.access: Paid entry, around EUR 1 (often free on Sundays), open weekdays 09:30-17:30, Sundays and holidays 10:30-17:30
trees.transport: Monte parish, reachable by the Monte cable car from Funchal plus a short walk, or by bus toward Monte. No car needed for this one.
trees.notes: Register entry ASMAC n.100 (island code FMFSp01). Height 36.0m, maximum perimeter 3.52m (352cm), notable reason 'Tamanho' (size), condition 'Bom' (good). No age reference in the register. The estate, formerly Quinta do Monte, is where the exiled Emperor Karl I of Austria-Hungary lived and died in 1922; the register's historical notes describe the quinta's history, and a tree reportedly planted to mark Napoleon Bonaparte's passage into his own exile is mentioned for the estate generally but NOT tied to this specific beech, so that anecdote is deliberately left out of the story entirely rather than repeated near it, per the bridge-claim rule. Second source: TripAdvisor reviews and madeiralovers.com confirm the garden is real, open to paying visitors, with the stated hours and fee, corroborating the site but not the specific beech (same site-level caveat as mdr_001/002). Alive: garden operating and reviewed as of 2026. No best_time set: the phenology file rates European beech autumn colour highly, but this specimen sits at 32.6N in a permanently humid cloud belt at the extreme edge of the species' range and no source describes its colouring, so an invented peak was avoided.
trees.how_to_recognise: Thirty-six metres of purple-leaved beech on a 3.5-metre trunk, dominating the garden and the only northern forest tree in it.

trees.name: The Douglas Fir of Queimadas
trees.story:
A Douglas fir has no business in a laurel forest, and this one is 39 metres tall. It is the tallest tree on this list, a North American conifer planted inside Parque Florestal das Queimadas, which sits in the laurisilva that UNESCO listed as World Heritage: the largest surviving remnant of the laurel forest that once covered much of southern Europe. Madeira's register lists it for size at 3.61 metres round, condition good, age no reference.

Worth being straight about what it is. Nothing here is native, and it is on this page because it is a genuinely large specimen at a place people already come to, not because it belongs to the forest around it.

That place is the trailhead for PR9, the Levada do Caldeirao Verde, one of the walks that brings people to Madeira in the first place, and the register calls Queimadas one of the most visited sites on the island. The park is free and open, with the levada path running off into the laurel.

Nobody has dated the fir, and there is a reason not to guess from its height: Douglas firs grow fast, so a big one need not be an old one. If you find a planting record, send it.
trees.transport: By car from Funchal via Santana, roughly 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes of driving; there is no practical public transport to the park, so a car is the realistic way.
trees.notes: Register entry ASMAC n.97 (island code SSPM01). Height 39.0m, maximum perimeter 3.61m (361cm), notable reason 'Tamanho' (size), condition 'Bom' (good). No age reference in the register. Queimadas Forest Park is the well-known trailhead for PR9, the Levada do Caldeirao Verde walk, and sits inside Madeira's laurisilva UNESCO area; the register notes it as one of the most visited sites on the island. Second source (TripAdvisor plus AllTrails and visitmadeira.com) confirms the park is real, free, and actively visited in 2026, but describes the park generally rather than this specific Douglas fir, so flagged as site-level corroboration only, same caveat as the other register entries. Alive: park in active public use in 2026. This is a planted exotic conifer inside a native-forest park, included on the size/register merit alone, not as a laurisilva specimen, and the story says so outright.
trees.how_to_recognise: At the PR9 trailhead, a 39-metre conifer standing in laurel forest, which is the whole reason it is impossible to miss.

trees.name: The Witch Tree of Fanal

location.address: Fanal, Paul da Serra plateau, Ribeira da Janela, Porto Moniz (within the officially designated Nucleo de Tis - Fanal)

trees.story:
The grove these trees belong to was already standing when the Portuguese found Madeira uninhabited in 1419. Fanal is a protected 20-hectare nucleus of til, Ocotea foetens, on the Paul da Serra plateau inside the UNESCO laurel forest, and the island's register dates it only as centenas de anos, hundreds of years, referencing a stand that predates settlement. The eight trunks the surveyors measured run from 0.68 to 2.28 metres round.

One tree in it has become the one everybody photographs. Travel and photography sources call it the Witch Tree, arvore da bruxa, for a trunk that twists hard and limbs that read as outstretched arms under a coat of moss. Tourist literature puts it at 500 or 600 years; the register will say no more than hundreds, and neither figure rests on a measurement, so this page does not sharpen it.

Nothing on the ground names it. There is no sign, no arrow and no path to the trunk, and visitors regularly report hunting around the grove before they find it, which is why our pin marks the area rather than the tree. Come in the morning fog if you can. That is when Fanal looks the way it does in the photographs, and when the tis stop reading as trees.
trees.access: Free, public land inside the Madeira Natural Park, rated 'muito facil' (very easy) by the register; a short walk from the Fanal parking area, but there is no on-site signage naming or pointing to this specific tree
trees.transport: By car only; roughly 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes from Funchal via the ER209, and well over an hour back, because Paul da Serra is mountain plateau driving rather than a suburban hop.
trees.notes: The til grove at Fanal is officially designated as 'Nucleo de Tis - Fanal' (ASMAC n.77, island code PMRJOF01, register coordinates 32.809278,-17.141472), a 20-hectare nucleus of Ocotea foetens inside the laurisilva UNESCO World Heritage area, documented with 8 trunk perimeters (2.28, 2.27, 1.43, 0.68, 1.59, 1.05, 1.54 and 1.47m) and age given only as 'centenas de anos' (hundreds of years), referenced as predating Madeira's 1419 settlement. That register entry alone would be a grove, not a collectible point. However, one specific specimen within this nucleus is independently and repeatedly identified across multiple travel and photography sources as the 'Witch Tree' or 'arvore da bruxa': a single ancient til with a dramatically twisted, moss-hung trunk and limbs read as outstretched arms, treated as Fanal's single most photographed tree (mymodernmet.com, journeyera.com, beyondmadeira.com which has a page dedicated to this one tree, rexby.com). A community-contributed OpenStreetMap node (id 11893400096) independently tags this exact spot 'Witch tree' with denotation=natural_monument, roughly 350m from the register's stated nucleus coordinate, i.e. within the same grove area. Combining the official register (existence, species, protected status, rough age) with the independent OSM identification plus multiple independent travel/photography write-ups (identity, fame, appearance) clears the two-source bar for THIS specimen, distinct from the grove as a whole. Flagged and location_precision approximate rather than confirmed because sources explicitly warn there is no signage and visitors 'need to search and guess' to find it, so the pin should be read as 'this area of the grove', not a surveyed trunk position, and the story says exactly that. Age_min/max is a broad band reflecting tourism-source claims of '500 to 600 years' against the register's vaguer 'hundreds of years'; treated as an estimate repeated no more precisely than the sources allow, not a derived calculation, and the story keeps the grove's pre-1419 dating separate from the individual tree's band. Alive: multiple 2024-2026 travel and photography posts describe visiting it recently; Madeira's 2016 wildfire is known to have reached parts of the island's laurisilva but no source reports damage to this specific grove or tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: A hard-twisted trunk with limbs reading as outstretched arms under a coat of moss. Nothing on the ground names it and there is no path to it, so the pin marks the grove rather than the tree.

trees.name: The Dragon Tree Grove of Neves

location.address: Jardim do Nucleo dos Dragoeiros das Neves, Caminho da Portada, Sitio das Neves, Sao Goncalo, Funchal

trees.story:
The Regional Government of Madeira bought this piece of land for one reason: the trees standing on it. The Nucleo dos Dragoeiros das Neves is a small purpose-built garden in Sao Goncalo, five kilometres out of central Funchal, laid out around what the island's register calls a notable group of centenary dragon trees. It has an information centre, opening hours, a phone number and guided visits available on request, which is remarkable treatment for a garden you can cross in a minute, and it tells you how little of Madeira's original dragon tree population is left.

Dracaena draco is native here and to the Canaries and almost nowhere else, and it grows slowly enough to make the register's word centenarios mean something: roughly ten years to reach two or three metres. The thickest trunk in the group measures 4.77 metres around and the stand reaches 13 metres. The register gives no age beyond centenary, and this page invents none.

Cut the bark and the sap runs red. That is dragon's blood, imported into Europe for centuries as a dye, a varnish and a medicine, and the trees were tapped hard for it. Entry is free, the information centre keeps weekday hours, and the whole visit takes twenty minutes.
trees.access: Free entry, public garden with an information centre open Monday-Friday 09:00-12:30 and 14:00-17:30; guided visits available by contacting the centre
trees.transport: About 5 km from central Funchal by road; no direct public transport noted, so a taxi or car is the realistic way.

photo.attribution: Paulo SP/ Wikimedia, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: Register entry ASMAC n.86 (island code FSGDD01): 'Nucleo de Dragoeiros', height 13.0m, maximum perimeter 4.77m (477cm), age 'Sem referencia' but description calls the group 'um notavel grupo de dragoeiros centenarios' (a notable group of centenary dragon trees), so 'over a century' is repeated as vaguely as the register states it, not sharpened. Purpose-built conservation garden acquired by the Regional Government of Madeira specifically to protect this group; unlike the Fanal til nucleus this is a compact, purpose-built, named garden (not a stretch of forest) with its own official IFCN information centre page confirming address, phone, opening hours and free access, independently corroborated by the tourism board (visitmadeira.com). Treated as ONE ensemble entry under the rule that allows a compact famous grouping with one obvious place to stand: the garden itself, not any single trunk, is the destination, and it is signposted and staffed, unlike Fanal's informally-nicknamed specimen. Dragon trees are native to Madeira and the Canaries and slow-growing (roughly 10 years to reach 2-3m per IFCN), consistent with 'centenary' framing. Alive: information centre and garden actively described as operating in 2026 sources. No best_time: dragon trees flower and fruit irregularly and look much the same year-round.
trees.how_to_recognise: A group rather than one tree, the thickest trunk 4.77 metres round and the stand reaching thirteen metres, in a garden you can cross in a minute.

trees.name: The Araucaria of Quinta Vigia

location.address: Quinta Vigia, Avenida do Infante 1, Se, Funchal

trees.story:
To see this one you walk into the official residence of the President of the Regional Government of Madeira, and nobody asks you anything at the gate. Quinta Vigia has been the president's house since 1984, and its grounds, about a hectare of them above the seafront on Avenida do Infante, stay open free of charge on weekdays, roughly half past eight until half past five. Monday to Friday only, so this one is a weekday errand.

The araucaria in those grounds sits on Funchal's own list of monumental trees, entered as code 292 in a table the city drew from a 2008 regional survey that recorded 118 remarkable specimens across the municipality, 111 of them classed monumental. What the table does not say is which araucaria it is. It gives the genus and stops there.

So we cannot tell you either, and we would rather say so than guess. One database files it as a Cook pine and cites nothing whatsoever for the claim; the garden's own description mentions Norfolk Island pine among the exotics growing here. The two are separable from below: a Norfolk Island pine stacks its branches in even tiers, a Cook pine leans in a narrower column. If you are standing under it and you know your araucarias, tell us which one this is.

Nobody has recorded its age or its girth either.
trees.access: Free entry, government grounds (official residence of the President of the Regional Government of Madeira), open to the public Monday to Friday, roughly 08:00/08:30 to 17:30/18:00 depending on source; closed weekends and holidays. No appointment needed to walk the gardens.
trees.transport: Avenida do Infante, central Funchal seafront; walkable (10-15 min) from Praca do Municipio, or a short bus/taxi ride. No car needed.
trees.notes: Officially designated as code 292 ("Araucaria") under Quinta Vigia in Quadro 5 of the Funchal PDM Relatorio de Fundamentacao (Volume II, March 2018), which itself cites the regional government publication "Arvores Monumentais e Emblematicas" (Direcao Regional de Florestas, 2008) as the source of the whole monumental-tree list for the municipality (118 specimens recensed, 111 monumental + 7 emblematic) -- one official register source. Second source: IFCN Madeira and visitmadeira.com/lifecooler.com independently confirm Quinta Vigia is a real, currently operating public garden (c.10,000 sqm), the official residence of the President of the Regional Government since 1984, open to the public free of charge on weekdays; these describe the garden and its general planting (which includes multiple araucaria and other exotic species) rather than this specific tree, so flagged as site-level corroboration, the same caveat already used on mdr_001-004 in this city file. SPECIES CAUTION: Wikidata (Q98858620) labels this specific specimen Araucaria columnaris but cites ZERO references for that claim; its own "described at" link points to a monumentaltrees.com page (height 41.20m, measured 2018-02-09) that this pass could not view (Cloudflare bot-check blocked both a plain fetch and a browser-session attempt, two tries). Per the search-summary rule, an unseen page is not evidence, so that height figure is NOT recorded here and the species is left at genus level rather than repeating an uncited claim -- the PDM table itself only says "Araucaria" with no species epithet, and IFCN prose about the garden separately mentions Araucaria heterophylla as one of several exotic species present at Quinta Vigia generally, so heterophylla vs columnaris is genuinely unresolved by this pass. The page should ask the reader which araucaria this is. Alive: garden in continuous active public/government use through 2026 per its own site and tourism sources. No girth or height recorded because the only figure found (monumentaltrees, via Wikidata) could not be verified on the source page itself. Write-time note: species deliberately left at genus level per the verification record, and the story states plainly that we do not know which araucaria this is and asks the reader; the 41.2m height reached via Wikidata is not used anywhere because its source page could not be read. No how_to_recognise, because the honest recognition question here is the unresolved species itself.

trees.name: The Ombu of the Municipal Garden

location.address: Jardim Municipal do Funchal, Rua Ivens 11, Se, Funchal

trees.story:
The fattest thing in this garden is not a tree. Phytolacca dioica, which Madeirans call bela-sombra, beautiful shade, is a giant herb out of the South American pampas: the swollen grey base that makes one look ancient is soft water-storing tissue rather than timber, it folds outward into what look like roots halfway up, and it grows fast enough that bulk says very little about years.

Funchal's list of monumental trees carries this one as code 305, from a table the municipality drew off a 2008 regional survey of the island's remarkable trees. No age, no girth, no height.

The garden around it earns the detour on its own. The Jardim Municipal opened in 1885 as the Jardim Dona Amelia on the ground of the old Convento de Sao Francisco, and those 8,300 square metres of former Franciscan enclosure are now a free public park in the middle of the city, gates reported open round the clock. Rua Ivens runs along the top of it.

One warning. The same garden holds a second monumental tree, a camphor, and both come through on the same map point, so you may meet the wrong one first. The soft grey non-wood is how you know you have the ombu. Nobody has dated either of them, and if you know when this one went in, tell us.
trees.access: Free, public municipal garden, open every day (reported as open around the clock); this specific tree sits somewhere within an 8,300 sqm garden rather than at a marked spot.
trees.transport: Central Funchal, Rua Ivens, a short walk from Avenida Arriaga and the seafront. No car needed.
trees.notes: Officially designated as code 305 ("Bela Sombra") under "Jardim Municipal do Funchal" in Quadro 5 of the Funchal PDM Relatorio de Fundamentacao (Volume II, March 2018), which cites the regional government publication "Arvores Monumentais e Emblematicas" (Direcao Regional de Florestas, 2008) as the source for the whole municipal monumental-tree list -- one official register source, same document used for mdr_007/009/010. Second source: the Portuguese Wikipedia article on the garden and the Camara Municipal do Funchal / visitfunchal pages independently confirm the Jardim Municipal do Funchal (formerly Jardim Dona Amelia, opened 1885 on the former Convento de Sao Francisco site) is a real, currently operating, free public garden at this exact address, bordered by Rua Ivens (north) and Rua Conselheiro Jose Silvestre Ribeiro (west), matching the Wikidata record street address for this tree; the Wikipedia article lists the garden general planting (barbusano, dragoeiro, til, pau-branco, kigelia, garcinia, plumeria, pandanus) but does not name the bela-sombra specifically, so flagged as site-level rather than tree-specific corroboration, same caveat pattern as the rest of this city file. LOCATION CAUTION: Wikidata gives the identical coordinate (32.647993,-16.912191) for BOTH this tree and the camphor tree (mdr_009) in the same garden, which reads as a single park-level point rather than two independently surveyed trunk positions, so both are marked approximate rather than confirmed. Garden is compact (8,300 sqm, roughly one hectare) so approximate still places a visitor within a short walk of the trunk. Alive: garden in continuous public use through 2026 per municipal and tourism sources. No girth or height found for this specific specimen; the parent 2008 survey likely records one but this pass could not access that book directly, only the PDM report that cites it. Species note: Phytolacca dioica is a South American species (Argentina/Uruguay/Brazil/Paraguay) unrelated to any Madeiran native, grown widely as a shade tree; the common Portuguese name means literally beautiful shade.
trees.how_to_recognise: A soft grey trunk that swells and folds outward into what look like roots halfway up. The garden's other monumental tree is a camphor, ordinary and woody beside it.

trees.name: The Camphor Tree of the Municipal Garden

location.address: Jardim Municipal do Funchal, Rua Conselheiro Jose Silvestre Ribeiro, Se, Funchal

trees.story:
Crush a leaf and you will know whether you have found the right tree. Cinnamomum camphora carries camphor in its leaves and its wood, and the smell is the giveaway, which matters here more than it usually would: this garden holds two monumental trees and both sit on the same map point.

The other is an ombu, a soft grey South American thing that is not really a tree in the botanical sense at all. This one is its opposite, an evergreen with a proper woody trunk that keeps its crown through the winter. Camphor is no more native to Madeira than the ombu is; Cinnamomum camphora comes from East Asia. It stands in a garden that mixes native and imported freely: Madeiran barbusano, til, pau-branco and dragon trees growing alongside kigelia, garcinia, plumeria and pandanus.

Funchal's monumental list has it as code 312, canforeira, in the table the municipality took from a 2008 regional survey of the island's remarkable trees. Nothing is recorded against it: no age, no girth, no height.

It grows in the Jardim Municipal, 8,300 square metres of public garden opened in 1885 on the ground of the old Convento de Sao Francisco, free and reported open at any hour, with Rua Conselheiro Jose Silvestre Ribeiro running down its western side. If you know when this one was planted, tell us.
trees.access: Free, public municipal garden, open every day (reported as open around the clock); this specific tree sits somewhere within an 8,300 sqm garden rather than at a marked spot.
trees.transport: Central Funchal, Rua Conselheiro Jose Silvestre Ribeiro side of the garden, a short walk from Avenida Arriaga and the seafront. No car needed.
trees.notes: Officially designated as code 312 ("Canforeira") under "Jardim Municipal do Funchal" in Quadro 5 of the Funchal PDM Relatorio de Fundamentacao (Volume II, March 2018), same official register as mdr_007/008/010, itself citing "Arvores Monumentais e Emblematicas" (Direcao Regional de Florestas, 2008). Second source: same as mdr_008, the Portuguese Wikipedia article plus visitfunchal/Camara Municipal pages independently confirm the garden is real, free, public and currently operating at this address; they do not name this specific camphor tree, so flagged as site-level rather than tree-specific corroboration. This is a DIFFERENT registered specimen from mdr_008 (different code, 312 vs 305, different species) even though Wikidata gives it the identical coordinate (32.647993,-16.912191) to the bela-sombra, which is why both are marked approximate: the shared coordinate reads as a single park-level point rather than two independently surveyed trunk positions. Garden is compact (8,300 sqm) so approximate still places a visitor within a short walk. Alive: garden in continuous public use through 2026. No girth or height found for this specific specimen. Camphor trees (Cinnamomum camphora) are already used elsewhere on this site under the canonical common name Camphor Tree; this entry matches that naming.
trees.how_to_recognise: An ordinary woody evergreen with a dense crown, and the crushed leaf smells of camphor. The garden's other monumental tree is an ombu, soft and grey and barely wood at all.

trees.name: The Pohutukawa of Quinta do Palheiro Ferreiro

location.address: Quinta do Palheiro Ferreiro (Palheiro Gardens), Caminho do Palheiro 32, Sao Goncalo, Funchal

trees.story:
Funchal's list of monumental trees names nine more entries inside this one garden: a tulip tree, a til, a Queensland araucaria, an oak, an Atlas cedar, a camphor tree, a sequoia, a Canary pine and groups of planes. The one this page picks is the New Zealander.

Metrosideros excelsa, the pohutukawa, grows wild on sea cliffs at the top of New Zealand's North Island and almost nowhere else, gripping rock with the aerial roots that hang off its older limbs. At home it flowers scarlet through the southern December, which is how it became New Zealand's Christmas tree. In Portugal it does the same thing in May and June, half a year out of step with its own name.

This specimen is code 192 on the municipal table, entered as Metrosidero under Quinta do Palheiro Ferreiro, from the same 2008 regional survey that supplies the rest of Funchal's list. It carries no age and no measurement of any kind.

Palheiro Gardens sits about 500 metres up in the hills east of the city, fifteen to twenty minutes by car or taxi, so this is the tree you plan a morning around rather than pass on a walk. Entry is 11 euros, six for residents and for anyone between fifteen and seventeen, free for children, and the gates open every day of the year except Christmas Day. If somebody has put a tape around this trunk, send us the number.

best_time.label: May and June, when the crown fills with red stamens

trees.access: Paid entry (Palheiro Gardens): adults EUR 11, ages 15-17 EUR 6, children free, Madeira residents EUR 6 with proof of residence; open daily 09:00-17:00, every day of the year except Christmas Day.
trees.transport: Caminho do Palheiro, in the hills east of Funchal (about 500m altitude); reachable by taxi or car, roughly 15-20 minutes from central Funchal, or bus toward Sao Goncalo/Camacha plus a walk.
trees.notes: Officially designated as code 192 ("Metrosidero") under "Quinta do Palheiro, Palheiro Ferreiro" in Quadro 5 of the Funchal PDM Relatorio de Fundamentacao (Volume II, March 2018), the same document and 2008 regional source used for mdr_007/008/009; Wikidata (Q98815233) cites this exact PDM PDF as its own reference, confirming the match. Second source: TripAdvisor and madeira-web.com independently confirm Quinta do Palheiro Ferreiro (Palheiro Gardens) is a real, currently operating, paid private estate garden open daily, admired for its exotic plant collection; they describe the garden generally and do not name this specific metrosideros, so flagged as site-level rather than tree-specific corroboration, same caveat as the rest of this pass and the existing city file. ACCESS: private estate but genuinely open to the paying public every day (except Christmas), which satisfies the access test the same way Madeira paid-entry hard rule cases already do (e.g. the Botanical Garden ginkgo, mdr_001); this is not a private residence closed to visitors. Note the same PDM table lists SEVERAL other named specimens at this same Quinta do Palheiro / Palheiro Ferreiro location (tulipeiro, til, another araucaria da Queenslandia, carvalho, cedro do Atlas, another canforeira, nucleos de platanos, sequoia, pinheiro das canarias) under separate codes, so this is one specimen among many monumental trees in the same garden, picked as the collectible point for this pass because Metrosideros excelsa (pohutukawa) is a striking and distinctive New Zealand species rarely seen on this list; a second visit could add more from the same garden as separate entries later. Alive: garden in continuous paid public operation through 2026 per current tourism sources. No girth or height found for this specific specimen; the parent 2008 survey likely records one but this pass could not access that book directly. Write-time note: best_time months [5,6] set to match the four Metrosideros excelsa entries already live on this site (cad_003, lis_017, por_023, sin_005), all recording a May/June flowering in Iberia. No Madeira-specific flowering date was found by the verify pass and no pohutukawa phenology file exists, so the label describes the species' Northern Hemisphere flowering rather than an observation of this specimen. No superlative claimed: Cadiz holds the oldest-documented-pohutukawa-in-Europe line and this tree has no measurement to rank on.
trees.how_to_recognise: A low spreading crown with curtains of aerial root off the older limbs, red with stamens in May and June. It is the only New Zealander among the garden's monumental trees.
